subject: Foods and Nutrition
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 3-hour practical test for 100 marks conducted by a visiting examiner. Candidates plan (with written time plan, ingredients and costs), prepare, cook and serve dishes or meals in response to a set question, and are marked on planning, methods of work, hygiene and safety, quality of results and presentation/service.

practicals.title: Simple chemical tests for starch, sugar, protein and fat
practicals.aim: To detect starch, reducing sugar, protein and fat in common Nigerian foodstuffs using simple chemical and physical tests.
apparatus: Stove or Bunsen burner / spirit lamp
Filter paper or plain brown paper
materials: Benedict's solution (or Fehling's A and B)
Biuret reagents (dilute sodium hydroxide and dilute copper(II) sulphate)
Food samples: garri or yam flour, ripe banana or pawpaw, glucose, egg white, groundnut, palm oil, bean flour
safety: Wear an apron; tie back long hair.
Point a heated test tube away from yourself and others.
Sodium hydroxide is corrosive - rinse any splash off the skin with plenty of water.
Keep ethanol away from naked flames.
Never taste any sample or reagent in the laboratory.
procedure: Prepare each solid sample by crushing about 1 g with a little water to form a suspension; label each test tube.
Starch: put a little of the sample on a white tile or in a test tube and add 2-3 drops of iodine solution. Note the colour.
Reducing sugar: put 2 cm³ of the food solution in a test tube, add 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution and heat in a boiling water bath for about 5 minutes. Note any colour change.
Protein: put 2 cm³ of the food solution in a test tube, add 2 cm³ of dilute sodium hydroxide, then add 1% copper(II) sulphate drop by drop, shaking gently. Note the colour.
Fat (grease-spot test): rub a little crushed groundnut on filter paper, allow to dry and hold the paper up to the light.
Fat (emulsion test): shake a little crushed sample with 2 cm³ of ethanol, pour the clear liquid into a test tube of water and note the appearance.
Run a control for each test using water only, and record all results in a table of Test / Observation / Inference.
practicals.expectedObservations: Iodine turns blue-black with garri or yam flour (starch present); it stays yellow-brown with egg white. Benedict's solution changes from blue through green and yellow to brick-red with glucose and ripe fruit (reducing sugar). Egg white and bean flour give a violet/purple colour in the Biuret test (protein). Groundnut and palm oil leave a translucent grease spot that does not dry off, and give a cloudy white emulsion in the ethanol test (fat). Water controls show no change.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Preparing reagents and samples by concentration. To make a 1% starch suspension, dissolve 1 g of starch in 100 cm³ of water (1 g / 100 cm³ x 100 = 1%). To make 50 cm³ of 2% glucose solution: mass needed = 2/100 x 50 = 1 g of glucose made up to 50 cm³. Results table example: Garri + iodine -> blue-black -> starch present; Glucose + Benedict's -> brick-red -> reducing sugar present; Egg white + Biuret -> violet -> protein present; Groundnut on paper -> translucent spot -> fat present.
precautions: Use clean test tubes for each sample to avoid contamination.
Heat Benedict's tests in a water bath, not directly over a flame.
Add copper(II) sulphate drop by drop; too much masks the violet colour.
Run a water control alongside each test.
sourcesOfError: Dirty test tubes carrying over a previous sample.
Heating for too short a time, giving a false negative for sugar.
Using too much copper(II) sulphate, giving a blue rather than violet colour.
Not letting the grease-spot paper dry, so water is mistaken for fat.
commonMistakes: Writing "positive" without stating the actual colour observed.
Confusing the inference (what is present) with the observation (what is seen).
Using iodine to test for sugar or Benedict's to test for starch.
Forgetting that sucrose (table sugar) is a non-reducing sugar and gives no brick-red colour without first being boiled with dilute acid and neutralised.
examTips: Set out results in three columns: Test, Observation, Inference - examiners award marks for each column.
Name the reagent precisely ("Benedict's solution", not "solution").
State the colour change fully, e.g. "blue to brick-red precipitate".
Mention a control and safety precautions when asked to describe the test.

checkQuestions.q: Which reagent is used to test for starch?
checkQuestions.explanation: Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch.

checkQuestions.q: A food solution heated with Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate. What does this show?
checkQuestions.explanation: A brick-red precipitate with Benedict's solution indicates a reducing sugar.

checkQuestions.q: What colour indicates protein in the Biuret test?
checkQuestions.explanation: Biuret reagent gives a violet or purple colour with protein.

checkQuestions.q: A translucent spot that does not dry off on paper indicates the presence of
checkQuestions.explanation: Fat leaves a permanent translucent grease spot; water evaporates.

practicals.title: Using a food composition table to analyse a meal
practicals.aim: To weigh the portions in a served meal and use a food composition table to calculate its energy and protein content.
apparatus: Kitchen scale (accurate to 1 g or 5 g)
Food composition table (per 100 g edible portion)
materials: A served meal, e.g. boiled rice, beef stew, fried plantain (dodo) and an orange
safety: Wash hands before handling food.
Keep hot food covered and serve promptly.
Use a dry plate on the scale to avoid spills on the electrical base.
procedure: Place an empty plate on the scale and set it to zero (tare).
Weigh each component of the meal separately and record the mass in grams.
Look up each food in the food composition table and record its energy (kcal) and protein (g) per 100 g.
Calculate the nutrient in each portion: value per 100 g x mass of portion / 100.
Add the values to find the total for the meal.
Compare the total with the recommended intake for the person being fed and suggest improvements.
practicals.expectedObservations: The meal provides most of its energy from the rice and fried plantain, while most of the protein comes from the beef. Fried foods show a high energy value because of absorbed oil.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Values given in the table (per 100 g): cooked rice 130 kcal, 2.7 g protein; beef stew 210 kcal, 20 g protein; fried plantain 250 kcal, 1.0 g protein; orange 47 kcal, 0.9 g protein. Portions weighed: rice 250 g, beef 80 g, plantain 100 g, orange 130 g. Energy: rice 130 x 250/100 = 325 kcal; beef 210 x 80/100 = 168 kcal; plantain 250 x 100/100 = 250 kcal; orange 47 x 130/100 = 61.1 kcal. Total energy = 804.1 kcal. Protein: 2.7 x 2.5 = 6.75 g; 20 x 0.8 = 16 g; 1.0 x 1.0 = 1.0 g; 0.9 x 1.3 = 1.17 g. Total protein = 24.92 g (about 25 g).
precautions: Use the "edible portion" values and weigh food without bones or peel where the table requires it.
Tare the scale before every weighing.
Use the cooked-food values for cooked foods - raw and cooked values differ.
sourcesOfError: Food composition values are averages and differ from the actual food.
Oil absorbed in frying varies from batch to batch.
Scale reading errors with small portions.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by 100 when the table is per 100 g.
Using raw rice values for cooked rice.
Adding up portions with different units (kJ and kcal).
examTips: Show the formula, the substitution and the answer with units for each food.
Round only at the end.
If asked to improve the meal, link your suggestion to a nutrient, e.g. "add ugwu (fluted pumpkin) leaves for vitamins A and iron".

checkQuestions.q: Cooked rice provides 130 kcal per 100 g. How much energy is in a 200 g portion?
Why should cooked-food values be used for cooked rice?
options: Cooked rice contains absorbed water, so its nutrients per 100 g are lower
Cooked rice weighs less than raw rice
checkQuestions.explanation: Cooked rice has absorbed water, which dilutes the nutrients per 100 g.

checkQuestions.q: In the worked example, which food supplied the most protein?
checkQuestions.explanation: Beef supplied 16 g of the 24.92 g total.

practicals.title: Planning, costing and preparing a family meal
practicals.aim: To plan, cost, prepare and serve a balanced dinner for a family of five following the principles of meal planning.
materials: Fresh tomatoes, tomato paste, pepper and onions
Cabbage, carrots and cucumber for salad
safety: Turn pan handles inwards away from the edge of the cooker.
Use separate boards for raw chicken and salad vegetables.
Cook chicken until juices run clear (core temperature at least 75 °C).
Wipe up spills immediately.
procedure: Read the question carefully and note the number of people, the meal and any special needs.
Choose dishes that include all classes of food and give variety of colour, texture and flavour, e.g. jollof rice, fried chicken, vegetable salad and fresh fruit.
Write a list of ingredients with quantities and calculate the cost.
Write an order of work (time plan) showing when each dish is started so that everything is ready to serve hot at the same time.
Prepare and cook the dishes, tasting and adjusting seasoning; wash up as you go.
Dish up neatly with garnish, set the table and serve at the stated time.
Clean the work area and evaluate the meal.
practicals.expectedObservations: A well-planned meal is served on time, hot food is hot and cold food is cold, colours contrast (red jollof, green salad, golden chicken), and the work area stays tidy throughout.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Costing for five people (illustrative prices): rice 750 g at N2,000/kg = N1,500; chicken 1 kg = N5,000; tomatoes, pepper and paste = N1,200; vegetable oil 150 ml at N3,000/litre = N450; onions and seasoning = N600; salad vegetables = N1,000. Total = N9,750. Cost per person = 9,750 / 5 = N1,950. Time plan: 10:00 wash and season chicken; 10:20 boil chicken; 10:45 prepare stew base; 11:10 add rice to jollof; 11:20 fry chicken; 11:40 prepare salad; 12:00 dish up and serve.
precautions: Buy and use quantities that match the number of people to avoid waste.
Prepare cold dishes last or keep them chilled.
Keep a clean cloth for wiping hands.
sourcesOfError: Market prices change, so the cost is only an estimate.
Cooking times vary with the heat of the stove.
commonMistakes: Choosing dishes that are all starchy or all one colour.
No time plan, so some food is cold when served.
Leaving washing-up until the end.
Forgetting a drink or dessert when the question asks for a complete meal.
examTips: The visiting examiner marks planning, method of work, hygiene, results (taste, appearance) and serving - all count.
Write your plan clearly and stick to it; examiners compare your work against your time plan.
Present dishes on clean plates with suitable garnish and serve at the exact time stated.

checkQuestions.q: A meal costs N9,750 for five people. What is the cost per person?
Why is an order of work (time plan) important in a cookery practical?
options: It ensures dishes are ready to serve at the right time and temperature
It reduces the number of dishes
checkQuestions.explanation: The time plan co-ordinates the dishes so they are ready together.

checkQuestions.q: Which addition best improves the colour and vitamin content of jollof rice and chicken?
checkQuestions.explanation: A vegetable salad adds colour contrast and vitamins and minerals.

practicals.title: Planning a meal for a person with diabetes
practicals.aim: To plan and prepare a lunch for an adult with diabetes, controlling the carbohydrate content and choosing foods that raise blood sugar slowly.
safety: Wash hands and vegetables thoroughly.
Remove fish bones carefully before serving.
Use oven gloves when draining hot water.
procedure: State the dietary needs: controlled carbohydrate spread through the day, high fibre, little sugar and fat, regular meals.
Choose foods: boiled unripe plantain, vegetable soup with fish, and an orange instead of a sweet drink.
Weigh the carbohydrate foods so that the meal provides about 45-60 g carbohydrate.
Boil the plantain in its skin, prepare the vegetable soup with very little oil, and steam or boil the fish.
Serve a measured portion and offer water to drink.
Evaluate the meal against the needs listed.
practicals.expectedObservations: The meal is filling, colourful and low in sugar and fat. Unripe plantain is firm and less sweet than ripe plantain because more of its carbohydrate is starch rather than sugar.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Carbohydrate (given values per 100 g): boiled unripe plantain 31 g; orange 12 g; vegetable soup about 3 g per portion. Portions: plantain 120 g -> 31 x 120/100 = 37.2 g; orange 130 g -> 12 x 130/100 = 15.6 g; soup 3 g. Total = 37.2 + 15.6 + 3 = 55.8 g, which is within the 45-60 g target for the meal.
precautions: Avoid adding sugar to drinks or sauces.
Use measured oil (1-2 teaspoons) rather than pouring freely.
Serve meals at regular times.
sourcesOfError: Carbohydrate values in tables are averages.
Ripeness of the plantain changes its sugar content.
commonMistakes: Removing all carbohydrate - people with diabetes still need carbohydrate, in controlled amounts.
Frying the plantain instead of boiling it.
Serving a sweetened drink.
examTips: Begin with a short statement of the nutritional needs, then justify each dish against them.
Show portion sizes in grams.
Mention fibre-rich foods such as beans, vegetables and whole grains.

checkQuestions.q: Which choice is most suitable for a person with diabetes?
options: Ripe fried plantain with a soft drink
Boiled unripe plantain with vegetable soup and water
checkQuestions.explanation: Boiled unripe plantain with vegetables is high in fibre and low in sugar and fat.

checkQuestions.q: 120 g of boiled unripe plantain contains 31 g carbohydrate per 100 g. How much carbohydrate is in the portion?
Why should a person with diabetes eat meals at regular times?
options: To reduce the need for water
checkQuestions.explanation: Regular meals help to avoid large rises and falls in blood sugar.

practicals.title: Planning a kitchen layout (work triangle)
practicals.aim: To draw a scaled plan of a modern kitchen and check that the work triangle between sink, cooker and refrigerator is efficient.
materials: Measurements of the school or home kitchen
safety: Do not stand on worktops to measure; ask for help with high measurements.
procedure: Measure the length and width of the kitchen and the positions of doors and windows.
Choose a scale, e.g. 1 cm on paper = 20 cm (1:20), and draw the outline.
Mark the sink (near the window for light and drainage), the cooker and the refrigerator.
Join the centres of the three work centres to form the work triangle and measure each side.
Convert the measurements to real distances and add them up.
Check that the total is within the recommended range and that no traffic route crosses the triangle; adjust if necessary.
Label all fixtures and add a key.
practicals.expectedObservations: An efficient kitchen has a work triangle with a total perimeter of roughly 4-8 m, each side between about 1.2 m and 2.7 m, with the cooker away from the door and not under a window.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Scale 1:20. Measured on paper: sink to cooker 9.0 cm, cooker to refrigerator 10.5 cm, refrigerator to sink 12.0 cm. Real distances: 9.0 x 20 = 180 cm = 1.8 m; 10.5 x 20 = 210 cm = 2.1 m; 12.0 x 20 = 240 cm = 2.4 m. Total = 1.8 + 2.1 + 2.4 = 6.3 m, which lies within the 4-8 m range, so the layout is efficient.
precautions: Use a sharp pencil and a consistent scale.
State the scale on the drawing.
Measure to the centre of each fitting.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate tape readings.
Rounding when converting between scale and real distances.
commonMistakes: Drawing without a scale.
Placing the cooker beside the door or under a window where curtains can catch fire.
Placing the refrigerator next to the cooker.
examTips: A neat, labelled and scaled plan earns more marks than a large untidy one.
Give reasons for the position of each work centre.

checkQuestions.q: On a 1:20 plan, a line of 9 cm represents
The three points of the kitchen work triangle are
checkQuestions.explanation: The work triangle links the sink, cooker and refrigerator.

checkQuestions.q: Why should a cooker not be placed under a window?
options: Curtains may catch fire and wind may blow out the flame
checkQuestions.explanation: Curtains and draughts near a cooker are fire and safety hazards.

practicals.title: Use, care and storage of kitchen equipment
practicals.aim: To identify common kitchen equipment, use it correctly and clean, descale and store it properly.
safety: Unplug electrical appliances before cleaning; never put the base of a kettle or blender into water.
Wash knives separately and never leave them in soapy water.
Dry hands before touching switches.
procedure: Identify each item and state its use and the material it is made of.
Scrape off food residue and soak saucepans in warm soapy water.
Wash in hot soapy water in order: glassware, cutlery, crockery, then pots and pans; rinse in clean hot water.
Clean the non-stick pan with a soft sponge only; scour aluminium gently with a mild abrasive.
Descale the kettle: fill with a 1:1 vinegar-water mixture, boil, leave for 30 minutes, then rinse and boil clean water twice before use.
Scrub the wooden board with hot soapy water along the grain, rinse and stand on its edge to dry.
Dry everything thoroughly and store: knives in a block or rack, heavy pans on low shelves.
practicals.expectedObservations: Scale (white chalky deposit) dissolves in vinegar with slight fizzing; cleaned equipment is free of grease and odour; the non-stick coating is undamaged.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Descaling solution for a 1.0 litre kettle filled half-way (500 ml) with a 1:1 mixture: vinegar = 1/2 x 500 = 250 ml; water = 250 ml. Refrigerator check: readings over a week of 3, 4, 4, 5 and 4 °C give a mean of 20/5 = 4 °C, within the safe 0-5 °C range.
precautions: Never use metal spoons or scourers on non-stick surfaces.
Rinse thoroughly after descaling so that food does not taste of vinegar.
Store equipment dry to prevent rust and mould.
sourcesOfError: Hard scale may need a second treatment.
Thermometer placed near the door reads high.
commonMistakes: Immersing electrical bases in water.
Soaking wooden spoons for long periods so they split.
Using abrasive powder on non-stick pans.
examTips: For each item state: name, material, use, and care - examiners often ask all four.
Mention unplugging before cleaning any electrical appliance.

checkQuestions.q: Which cleaning agent is most suitable for removing scale from a kettle?
checkQuestions.explanation: Vinegar is a weak acid that dissolves the calcium carbonate scale.

checkQuestions.q: A non-stick frying pan should be cleaned with
options: a soft sponge and soapy water
checkQuestions.explanation: Abrasives scratch and remove the non-stick coating.

checkQuestions.q: In what order should items be washed up?
options: Glassware, cutlery, crockery, pots and pans
checkQuestions.explanation: Least greasy items first keep the water cleaner for longer.

practicals.title: Kitchen safety audit and simple first aid
practicals.aim: To inspect a kitchen for hazards, check the first aid box and practise first aid for minor burns and cuts.
safety: Practise first aid on a partner only as a demonstration - no real wounds.
Wear gloves when handling dressings.
procedure: Use a checklist to inspect the kitchen: floors, cooker, electrical sockets, gas cylinder, knives, fire blanket or extinguisher, exits.
Record each item as safe or unsafe, and state the hazard and the action needed.
Check the first aid box against a contents list and note missing or expired items.
Demonstrate first aid for a minor burn: cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes, remove rings, cover loosely with cling film or a sterile non-fluffy dressing.
Demonstrate first aid for a small cut: wash hands, rinse the cut, press with a clean pad to stop bleeding, apply a plaster.
Calculate the safety score and write a short report.
practicals.expectedObservations: Common hazards include wet floors, pan handles sticking out, overloaded sockets, a leaking gas hose and blunt knives. Cooling a burn quickly reduces pain and tissue damage.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Safety score = checks passed / total checks x 100. If 18 of 24 checks are passed: 18/24 x 100 = 75%. The six failed items must be corrected and the kitchen rechecked; a target of 100% should be set before practical work.
precautions: Do not apply butter, oil, toothpaste or palm kernel oil to burns.
Do not burst blisters.
Seek medical help for large or deep burns and for cuts that will not stop bleeding.
sourcesOfError: Hazards that are temporary (e.g. a wet floor) may be missed.
commonMistakes: Using ice or iced water on burns.
Applying local remedies such as raw egg or oil to burns.
Listing hazards without stating prevention.
examTips: Give cause, prevention and first aid for each accident - all three are commonly asked.
State the cooling time for burns (at least 20 minutes).

checkQuestions.q: What is the correct first aid for a minor burn?
options: Cool under cool running water for at least 20 minutes
checkQuestions.explanation: Cool running water reduces heat damage and pain.

checkQuestions.q: A kitchen passes 18 of 24 safety checks. Its score is
Which is a hazard that commonly causes falls in the kitchen?
checkQuestions.explanation: Wet or greasy floors cause slips and falls.

practicals.title: Personal, kitchen and food hygiene routine
practicals.aim: To carry out correct hand washing, prepare a disinfecting solution and clean and sanitise work surfaces before and after food preparation.
safety: Never mix bleach with other cleaners such as acids or ammonia - toxic gases form.
Wear gloves when handling bleach and work in a ventilated room.
Label the diluted solution.
procedure: Put on a clean apron and hair covering; remove jewellery; cover any cut with a blue or waterproof plaster.
Wash hands: wet, apply soap, rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and nails for at least 20 seconds; rinse and dry with a clean towel.
Clean the work surface with hot soapy water to remove dirt and grease, then rinse.
Prepare a 0.1% bleach solution and wipe or spray the clean surface; leave for the contact time stated on the label, then rinse food-contact surfaces with clean water.
Separate raw and cooked foods and use different boards and knives.
At the end, empty and wash the bin, sweep and mop the floor, and wash and dry cloths.
practicals.expectedObservations: Hands, surfaces and equipment are visibly clean, the kitchen smells fresh, and there is no food debris to attract flies, cockroaches or rats.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Diluting 5% household bleach to 0.1%: dilution factor = 5 / 0.1 = 50, so 1 part bleach is made up to 50 parts in total. For 1 litre (1,000 ml): bleach = 1,000 / 50 = 20 ml, water = 1,000 - 20 = 980 ml.
precautions: Clean before you disinfect - disinfectant does not work well on greasy dirt.
Make fresh bleach solution daily.
Keep cleaning chemicals away from food.
sourcesOfError: Bleach strength varies between brands and weakens with age.
commonMistakes: Using the same cloth for the floor and work surfaces.
Skipping the thumbs and nails when hand washing.
Wiping a surface with a dirty cloth after disinfecting.
examTips: Distinguish personal hygiene, kitchen hygiene and food hygiene clearly in answers.
Examiners look for hand washing at the start of the practical and clean-as-you-go throughout.

checkQuestions.q: How long should hands be rubbed with soap during hand washing?
checkQuestions.explanation: At least 20 seconds of rubbing is recommended.

checkQuestions.q: How much 5% bleach is needed to make 1 litre of 0.1% solution?
checkQuestions.explanation: 1,000 / 50 = 20 ml bleach made up to 1 litre.

checkQuestions.q: Why must bleach never be mixed with acid cleaners?
checkQuestions.explanation: Acids react with hypochlorite to release chlorine gas.

practicals.title: Effect of different cooking methods on yam
practicals.aim: To compare boiling, roasting and frying of yam and observe the effect of moist and dry heat on mass, texture, colour and flavour.
safety: Lower food gently into hot oil; never leave hot oil unattended.
Dry yam pieces before frying to stop spitting.
Use oven gloves for the oven and grill.
procedure: Peel and cut the yam into three equal 500 g batches of similar-sized pieces; keep them in water to stop browning.
Batch A: boil in salted water with the lid on until tender (about 20 minutes).
Batch B: roast in the oven or over the grill until tender and browned (about 40 minutes).
Batch C: dry the pieces and deep-fry in hot oil until golden (about 10 minutes).
Drain and weigh each cooked batch.
Compare colour, texture, flavour and time taken, and calculate the percentage change in mass.
practicals.expectedObservations: Boiled yam is soft, pale and slightly heavier because the starch absorbs water and gelatinises. Roasted yam is dry, browned (dextrinisation of starch) with a crisp outer layer and loses mass through evaporation. Fried yam is crisp, golden and loses water but absorbs some oil.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Percentage change in mass = (final - initial) / initial x 100. Boiled: (520 - 500)/500 x 100 = +4%. Roasted: (430 - 500)/500 x 100 = -14%. Fried: (410 - 500)/500 x 100 = -18%. Boiling takes about 20 minutes, frying about 10 minutes and roasting about 40 minutes.
precautions: Cut pieces to the same size so that they cook evenly.
Weigh all batches on the same scale.
Drain fried yam on kitchen paper before weighing.
sourcesOfError: Unequal piece sizes.
Variable heat from the stove or grill.
Water clinging to boiled yam increases its mass.
commonMistakes: Confusing moist heat (boiling, steaming, stewing) with dry heat (roasting, baking, grilling, frying).
Overcrowding the frying pan so the oil temperature falls and the yam becomes greasy.
examTips: State the effect of heat on the specific nutrient: starch gelatinises in moist heat and dextrinises in dry heat.
Give at least one advantage and one disadvantage of each method.

checkQuestions.q: Which of these is a moist-heat method of cooking?
checkQuestions.explanation: Steaming uses moist heat from steam.

checkQuestions.q: Yam pieces weighing 500 g weigh 430 g after roasting. What is the percentage change?
The browning of starch in dry heat is called
checkQuestions.explanation: Dry heat converts starch to dextrins, giving a brown colour.

checkQuestions.q: Why does boiled yam gain a little mass?
options: Starch granules absorb water and swell
checkQuestions.explanation: Starch absorbs water and gelatinises during boiling.

practicals.title: Preparing dishes from plantain and starchy roots
practicals.aim: To identify types of plantain and starchy roots and prepare fried plantain (dodo), plantain porridge and yam pottage, comparing oil uptake.
safety: Peel plantain on a board, cutting away from the hand.
Keep the oil at moderate heat and dry food before frying.
procedure: Identify unripe (green), semi-ripe and ripe (yellow/black) plantain and state a dish suitable for each.
Measure 500 ml of vegetable oil into the frying pan; slice 600 g ripe plantain diagonally and fry until golden on both sides.
Drain on kitchen paper, then pour the remaining oil back into the jug and record the volume.
Prepare unripe plantain porridge: cut, cook with palm oil, pepper, crayfish and vegetables until soft.
Prepare yam pottage in the same way using yam.
Dish up attractively and compare taste, colour and texture.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ripe plantain fries quickly to a sweet, golden-brown dodo because of its sugar content (caramelisation); unripe plantain stays firm and starchy. Some oil is absorbed during frying.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Oil absorbed = 500 ml - 460 ml remaining = 40 ml. Mass of oil = 40 ml x 0.92 g/ml = 36.8 g. Energy from absorbed oil = 36.8 g x 9 kcal/g = 331.2 kcal. Shared among 4 portions = 331.2 / 4 = 82.8 kcal of extra energy per portion.
precautions: Fry at the correct temperature - oil that is too cool soaks into the food.
Do not overcrowd the pan.
Allow oil to cool before measuring it back.
sourcesOfError: Oil remains on the pan surface and slotted spoon, so measured absorption is slightly high.
commonMistakes: Frying unripe plantain expecting dodo.
Slicing too thinly so plantain burns.
Adding vegetables too early so they lose colour and vitamins.
examTips: State the stage of ripeness and the dish it suits.
Mention nutritive value: plantain gives carbohydrate, potassium and vitamin A (ripe).

checkQuestions.q: Why does ripe plantain brown faster than unripe plantain when fried?
options: It has more sugar, which caramelises
checkQuestions.explanation: Ripening converts starch to sugar, which caramelises.

checkQuestions.q: 500 ml of oil was used; 460 ml remained after frying. How much was absorbed?
Which of the following is a starchy root?
checkQuestions.explanation: Cassava is a starchy root.

practicals.title: Raising agents: scones with and without baking powder
practicals.aim: To investigate the effect of a chemical raising agent (baking powder) on the rise of scones made by the rubbed-in method.
safety: Use oven gloves.
Keep the oven door closed during baking.
Let trays cool before handling.
procedure: Prepare two identical mixtures: 200 g plain flour, a pinch of salt, 50 g margarine, 25 g sugar.
Sieve the flour (and baking powder for batch B only: 2 level teaspoons) to trap air.
Rub the fat into the flour with the fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs.
Add milk gradually to form a soft dough; handle lightly.
Roll each dough to 1.5 cm thick, cut rounds of the same size and bake at 220 °C for 10-12 minutes.
Cool, measure the height of three scones from each batch and find the mean.
practicals.expectedObservations: Scones with baking powder are well risen, light and open-textured because carbon dioxide is released when the powder is moistened and heated. Scones without it are flat, dense and hard; they rise only slightly from steam and air.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mean height: batch A (no baking powder) 1.2 cm; batch B (baking powder) 2.6 cm. Percentage increase = (2.6 - 1.2)/1.2 x 100 = 116.7%. Fat is 50/200 = 1/4 of the flour mass, the usual proportion for scones.
precautions: Use the same oven shelf and baking time for both batches.
Roll both doughs to the same thickness.
Work quickly so the gas is not lost before baking.
sourcesOfError: Uneven oven temperature.
Uneven rolling thickness.
Different handling of the two doughs.
commonMistakes: Heavy kneading, which toughens scones.
Too much liquid giving a sticky, spreading dough.
Opening the oven early so the scones collapse.
examTips: Name the three raising agents: air (sieving, whisking, rubbing in), steam (liquid in hot oven) and carbon dioxide (baking powder, yeast).
Explain how each raises the mixture - expansion of gas on heating.

checkQuestions.q: Which gas is produced by baking powder?
checkQuestions.explanation: Baking powder releases carbon dioxide when moist and heated.

checkQuestions.q: Scones rise from 1.2 cm to 2.6 cm. What is the percentage increase?
Sieving flour mainly introduces which raising agent?
checkQuestions.explanation: Sieving traps air in the flour.

practicals.title: Making pouring batter (pancakes) and coating batter
practicals.aim: To prepare a pouring batter for pancakes and a coating batter for fish, and to scale a recipe.
safety: Heat the pan with a thin film of oil only.
Lower coated fish away from you into the oil.
procedure: Pouring batter: sieve 100 g flour and a pinch of salt; make a well and add 1 egg.
Add 250 ml milk gradually, beating to a smooth batter the consistency of single cream; leave to stand for 15-20 minutes.
Heat a lightly oiled pan, pour in one ladle of batter and tilt to coat the base thinly; cook until golden, toss or turn, and cook the other side.
Coating batter: use the same flour and egg with half the liquid (about 125 ml) to give a thicker batter.
Dry and season the fish, dip in the coating batter and shallow- or deep-fry until golden.
Serve pancakes with lemon and sugar or a fruit filling, and the fish hot.
practicals.expectedObservations: A pouring batter gives thin, lacy pancakes; a coating batter clings to the fish and forms a crisp, golden case. Standing the batter allows the starch to swell and gives lighter results.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Basic pancake batter (makes about 8): flour 100 g, egg 1, milk 250 ml. To make 24 pancakes the scale factor is 24/8 = 3: flour 300 g, eggs 3, milk 750 ml. Coating batter uses half the liquid: 125 ml for 100 g flour.
precautions: Add liquid gradually to avoid lumps.
Keep the pan at a steady moderate heat.
Dry fish well so the batter sticks.
sourcesOfError: Egg sizes vary, changing the consistency.
commonMistakes: Pouring in all the milk at once and getting lumps.
Too much batter in the pan giving thick, heavy pancakes.
Cooking at too low a heat so pancakes become leathery.
examTips: State the uses of each batter type: pouring (pancakes, Yorkshire pudding), coating (fritters, fish).
Puff-puff is a yeast batter - be ready to explain the difference.

checkQuestions.q: Which is the correct consistency of a pouring batter?
checkQuestions.explanation: Pouring batter is thin, like single cream.

checkQuestions.q: A recipe for 8 pancakes uses 250 ml milk. How much milk is needed for 24?
checkQuestions.explanation: Scale factor 3: 250 x 3 = 750 ml.

checkQuestions.q: Why is batter left to stand before cooking?
options: To let starch grains swell for a lighter result
checkQuestions.explanation: Standing allows starch to absorb liquid.

practicals.title: Cake making by the creaming method (Victoria sandwich)
practicals.aim: To make a sandwich cake by the creaming method and scale the recipe using the equal-weights rule.
safety: Use oven gloves.
Crack eggs into a separate cup first to check freshness.
procedure: Grease and line the tins; preheat the oven to 180 °C.
Weigh the eggs in their shells and weigh the same mass of fat, sugar and flour.
Cream the fat and sugar until light, pale and fluffy.
Beat in the eggs a little at a time, adding a spoonful of flour if the mixture begins to curdle.
Fold in the sieved flour gently with a metal spoon.
Divide equally between the tins, level, and bake for 20-25 minutes until well risen and springy.
Cool on a rack, sandwich with jam and dust with icing sugar.
practicals.expectedObservations: Creamed fat and sugar become pale and increase in volume as air is trapped. A well-made cake is evenly risen, golden, springy to the touch, and a skewer comes out clean.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Equal-weights rule: 2 eggs weigh about 100 g, so use 100 g each of fat, sugar and flour. For 3 eggs (about 150 g): 150 g fat, 150 g sugar, 150 g flour. Total mixture for 3 eggs = 150 x 4 = 600 g, so each of two tins takes 300 g.
precautions: Add eggs gradually to stop curdling.
Fold in flour lightly to keep the air.
Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes.
sourcesOfError: Oven temperature differences.
Uneven division between tins.
commonMistakes: Under-creaming, giving a heavy cake.
Beating hard after adding flour, which knocks out air.
Cake sinking because of too much raising agent or opening the oven too early.
examTips: Know the four basic cake methods (rubbed-in, creamed, whisked, melted) with one example each.
Describe tests for readiness: springy, shrinks from sides, skewer clean.

checkQuestions.q: In the creaming method, what is beaten together first?
checkQuestions.explanation: Fat and sugar are creamed together to trap air.

checkQuestions.q: If 3 eggs weigh 150 g, how much flour is needed for a Victoria sandwich?
checkQuestions.explanation: Equal weights: 150 g flour.

checkQuestions.q: What causes curdling when eggs are added?
checkQuestions.explanation: Adding egg too fast breaks the fat-sugar emulsion.

practicals.title: Shortcrust pastry: Nigerian meat pies
practicals.aim: To make shortcrust pastry using the half-fat-to-flour rule and use it for meat pies, then cost the batch.
safety: Cook the filling thoroughly and cool it before filling the pastry.
Use oven gloves.
procedure: Prepare the filling: fry onions, add minced beef, diced potatoes and carrots, seasoning and a little water; cook until tender, thicken slightly and cool.
Sieve 400 g flour and a pinch of salt; rub in 200 g margarine to fine breadcrumbs.
Add cold water a little at a time (about 80 ml) and mix to a firm dough; rest it in a cool place for 15 minutes.
Roll out to about 3 mm, cut 12 rounds, place filling on one half, dampen the edges, fold and seal with a fork.
Brush with beaten egg and bake at 200 °C for 25-30 minutes until golden.
Cool on a rack and calculate the cost per pie.
practicals.expectedObservations: Shortcrust pastry is short (crumbly), light and golden; the fat coats the flour particles and limits gluten formation. Too much water makes it hard and it shrinks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Ratio fat : flour = 1 : 2, so 400 g flour needs 200 g fat. Costing (illustrative): flour N640, margarine N700, minced beef 300 g N1,800, vegetables N700, egg N200, seasoning N150. Total = N4,190 for 12 pies. Cost per pie = 4,190 / 12 = N349.17. Selling at cost + 50% gives 349.17 x 1.5 = N523.75 (round to N525).
precautions: Keep fat, water and hands cool.
Handle the dough lightly and roll in one direction.
Seal edges well to prevent the filling leaking.
sourcesOfError: Flour absorbs different amounts of water.
Prices vary between markets.
commonMistakes: Overworking the dough, making tough pastry.
Using a hot filling that melts the fat.
Too much water, causing hard, shrunken pastry.
examTips: State the principles: cool ingredients, light handling, correct proportions, resting, hot oven.
Give examples of shortcrust dishes: meat pie, jam tarts, Cornish pasties.

checkQuestions.q: The proportion of fat to flour in shortcrust pastry is
checkQuestions.explanation: Half fat to flour: 1:2.

checkQuestions.q: Why should ingredients be kept cool when making shortcrust pastry?
options: To prevent the fat melting and the pastry becoming greasy and tough
checkQuestions.explanation: Melted fat makes the pastry greasy and hard.

checkQuestions.q: A batch of 12 pies costs N4,190. The cost of one pie is about

practicals.title: Yeast mixtures: bread rolls and doughnuts
practicals.aim: To prepare a yeast dough, observe fermentation and make bread rolls (and doughnuts from the same principle).
apparatus: Clean damp cloth or cling film
safety: Use warm (about 37 °C), not hot, water.
Take care when deep-frying doughnuts; keep a lid nearby.
procedure: Mix the yeast with a little of the warm water and sugar; leave for 10 minutes until frothy.
Sieve 500 g flour and 10 g salt; rub in 25 g margarine and add the remaining sugar.
Add the yeast liquid and the rest of the 300 ml warm water; mix to a soft dough.
Knead on a floured board for about 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and leave in a warm place to rise until doubled in size (about 1 hour).
Knock back, divide into 12 equal pieces, shape into rolls, prove again for 15-20 minutes.
Glaze and bake at 220 °C for 12-15 minutes until they sound hollow when tapped.
practicals.expectedObservations: The yeast liquid becomes frothy; the dough becomes smooth and stretchy after kneading (gluten development) and doubles in size as carbon dioxide is produced by fermentation. Baked rolls are golden and sound hollow underneath.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Dough mass = 500 + 7 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 300 = 867 g. Each of 12 rolls = 867 / 12 = 72.25 g (about 72 g). Baker's percentages: salt 10/500 x 100 = 2%; yeast 7/500 x 100 = 1.4%; water 300/500 x 100 = 60%.
precautions: Do not let salt touch the yeast directly in concentrated form.
Warmth, food (sugar) and moisture are needed for yeast; too much heat kills it.
Prove in a warm, draught-free place.
sourcesOfError: Room temperature changes the rising time.
Old yeast may be inactive.
commonMistakes: Using hot water and killing the yeast.
Under-kneading, giving a heavy close texture.
Over-proving so the rolls collapse.
examTips: Know the conditions for yeast growth: warmth, moisture, food, time.
Explain the terms kneading, proving and knocking back.

checkQuestions.q: Which gas makes yeast dough rise?
checkQuestions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugar, producing carbon dioxide.

checkQuestions.q: What is the best water temperature for activating yeast?
checkQuestions.explanation: Blood heat (about 37 °C) suits yeast.

checkQuestions.q: A dough of 867 g is divided into 12 rolls. Each roll weighs about
Kneading the dough mainly
checkQuestions.explanation: Kneading develops elastic gluten strands.

practicals.title: Preparing and using butter icing and royal icing
practicals.aim: To prepare butter icing and royal icing to the correct consistency and use them to decorate a cake with piped designs.
apparatus: Piping bags and nozzles (star and writing)
safety: Use pasteurised egg white or dried egg albumen where possible, as royal icing is not cooked.
Keep icing covered to prevent contamination.
procedure: Butter icing: cream 100 g butter until soft, then gradually beat in 200 g sieved icing sugar and a few drops of milk or flavouring.
Colour part of the icing as required.
Royal icing: lightly whisk 1 egg white, then beat in about 250 g sieved icing sugar a spoonful at a time with a few drops of lemon juice until it stands in soft peaks.
Coat the cake with butter icing using a palette knife dipped in hot water for a smooth finish.
Fill a piping bag with royal icing and pipe borders, stars and lettering.
Allow the royal icing to set and evaluate neatness and finish.
practicals.expectedObservations: Butter icing is soft and creamy and spreads easily; royal icing is white and glossy, holds its shape when piped and sets hard on drying.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Butter icing ratio butter : icing sugar = 1 : 2 (100 g : 200 g). Royal icing: about 250 g icing sugar per egg white. For 3 egg whites: 3 x 250 = 750 g icing sugar. To ice a cake needing 450 g of butter icing: butter = 450 / 3 = 150 g, icing sugar = 300 g.
precautions: Always sieve icing sugar to remove lumps that block nozzles.
Keep royal icing covered with a damp cloth.
Cool the cake completely before icing.
sourcesOfError: Egg white size changes the amount of sugar needed.
Humidity affects setting.
commonMistakes: Icing a warm cake so the icing melts.
Adding liquid too quickly, making runny icing.
Overfilling the piping bag.
examTips: Name the types of icing and give uses of each.
Neat, even piping and a clean board earn presentation marks.

checkQuestions.q: The ratio of butter to icing sugar in butter icing is usually
checkQuestions.explanation: 1 part butter to 2 parts icing sugar.

checkQuestions.q: Royal icing is made from icing sugar, lemon juice and
checkQuestions.explanation: Egg white gives royal icing its hard setting quality.

checkQuestions.q: Why is icing sugar sieved?
checkQuestions.explanation: Lumps spoil smoothness and block nozzles.

practicals.title: Preparing tea, cocoa drink and zobo
practicals.aim: To prepare and serve tea, a cocoa drink and zobo (roselle drink) following the principles of beverage preparation.
safety: Pour boiling water carefully away from the body.
Use boiled and cooled water to make cold drinks.
procedure: Tea: warm the pot, add 1 teaspoon of tea per cup, pour on freshly boiling water, infuse 3-5 minutes and strain. Serve with milk and sugar separately.
Cocoa: blend 2 level teaspoons cocoa and sugar to a paste with a little cold milk, add hot milk (about 250 ml per cup) and bring just to the boil, stirring.
Zobo: wash 100 g dried roselle, boil in 2 litres water with ginger and cloves for 15-20 minutes, add pineapple peel for flavour, cool and strain.
Sweeten the zobo lightly, chill, and serve in clean glasses.
Lay a tray neatly and serve the beverages.
practicals.expectedObservations: Tea is clear and amber; cocoa is smooth without lumps because the powder was first blended to a paste; zobo is a deep red, slightly sour drink.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Zobo yield: 2 litres water reduced by evaporation and absorption to about 1.8 litres. Number of 250 ml glasses = 1,800 / 250 = 7.2, so 7 full servings. Cocoa for 6 cups: 2 x 6 = 12 level teaspoons and 6 x 250 = 1,500 ml milk.
precautions: Use freshly boiled water for tea - water that has boiled for long tastes flat.
Blend cocoa to a paste first to avoid lumps.
Strain drinks through a clean cloth.
sourcesOfError: Evaporation varies with heat and time, changing the zobo yield.
commonMistakes: Over-infusing tea so it becomes bitter.
Adding cocoa powder straight to hot milk, causing lumps.
Over-sweetening zobo.
examTips: State the principles: correct quantities, correct temperature, correct time, cleanliness, attractive serving.
Classify each drink (stimulating, nourishing, refreshing).

checkQuestions.q: Why is cocoa blended with cold milk before hot milk is added?
checkQuestions.explanation: Blending to a paste separates the starch grains and prevents lumps.

checkQuestions.q: How many 250 ml glasses can be filled from 1.8 litres of zobo?
checkQuestions.explanation: 1,800 / 250 = 7.2, so 7 full glasses.

checkQuestions.q: Tea and coffee are classified as
checkQuestions.explanation: They contain caffeine, a stimulant.

practicals.title: Preserving vegetables by drying
practicals.aim: To preserve okra and pepper by sun- or solar-drying and calculate the percentage of water removed.
apparatus: Clean drying trays or raised mesh racks
safety: Cover trays to keep off flies, dust and animals.
Wash hands after cutting hot peppers and avoid touching the eyes.
procedure: Select fresh, firm, undamaged vegetables; wash and drain.
Weigh the prepared okra and record the fresh mass.
Slice thinly and evenly; blanching briefly in boiling water helps keep colour.
Spread in a single layer on raised trays, cover with net and dry in the sun (or a solar dryer), turning daily and bringing in at night.
Continue until brittle (okra) or crisp (pepper), usually 3-5 days.
Weigh again and calculate the water lost; cool and store in airtight labelled jars.
practicals.expectedObservations: Slices shrink, darken slightly and become brittle. Dried okra keeps for months in an airtight container because micro-organisms and enzymes cannot act without water.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Fresh okra 1,500 g; dried okra 165 g. Water removed = 1,500 - 165 = 1,335 g. Percentage moisture removed = 1,335 / 1,500 x 100 = 89%.
precautions: Slice evenly so all pieces dry at the same rate.
Do not dry on bare ground.
Store only when completely dry, otherwise mould grows.
sourcesOfError: Humidity and rain slow drying.
Uneven slice thickness.
commonMistakes: Storing before fully dry.
Drying in thick layers.
Leaving trays uncovered.
examTips: Explain the principle: removing water stops micro-organisms and enzymes.
List other methods: smoking, salting, sugar (jam), freezing, canning, chemical preservatives.

checkQuestions.q: Drying preserves food mainly because
options: it kills all bacteria by heat
checkQuestions.explanation: Removal of water stops microbial growth and enzyme action.

checkQuestions.q: 1,500 g of okra dries to 165 g. The percentage moisture removed is
Why should drying vegetables be covered with net?
options: To keep off flies and dust
To keep them warm at night
checkQuestions.explanation: Covering prevents contamination.

practicals.title: Preserving fruit with sugar: pineapple jam
practicals.aim: To make pineapple jam, test for setting point and calculate the expected yield.
materials: Lemon or lime juice (adds acid and pectin)
safety: Boiling jam is very hot and sticky - stir with a long spoon and keep children away.
Handle hot jars with a cloth.
procedure: Sterilise jars by washing and heating in the oven or boiling water.
Peel, core and finely chop or grate 1 kg of pineapple; simmer with a little water and the lemon juice until soft.
Add 750 g sugar and stir over low heat until dissolved.
Boil rapidly, stirring occasionally, until setting point (about 104-105 °C).
Test: put a little jam on a cold saucer; it is set if the surface wrinkles when pushed.
Remove scum, pour into hot jars, cover, label with name and date.
practicals.expectedObservations: The jam thickens and becomes glossy; at setting point it wrinkles on the cold saucer. The high sugar concentration prevents micro-organisms from growing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Traditional yield rule: jam yield = sugar mass x 1.66 (for about 60% sugar). 750 g x 1.66 = 1,245 g. This fills four 250 g jars (1,000 g) with 245 g left for a fifth jar.
precautions: Dissolve sugar completely before boiling to avoid crystals.
Do not overboil - jam darkens and becomes sticky.
Fill jars while hot and seal at once.
sourcesOfError: Pineapple is low in pectin, so setting may be soft.
Evaporation varies.
commonMistakes: Under-boiling, giving runny jam that ferments.
Using unsterilised jars, causing mould.
examTips: Give the principle: high sugar concentration draws water out of micro-organisms (osmosis).
State the setting tests: saucer (wrinkle), flake, thermometer.

checkQuestions.q: How does sugar preserve jam?
options: It removes water from micro-organisms by osmosis
checkQuestions.explanation: High sugar concentration withdraws water from microbes.

checkQuestions.q: Using the 1.66 rule, 750 g of sugar gives about how much jam?
A cold saucer test shows setting point when
checkQuestions.explanation: Wrinkling shows a set gel.

practicals.title: Setting a table cover and a tray
practicals.aim: To set a table for a three-course dinner and a tray for an invalid, using correct table appointments.
apparatus: Table and tablecloth or place mats
Dinner plates, side plates, soup bowls
safety: Carry glasses and crockery on a tray, not stacked in the hands.
Check crockery for chips and cracks.
procedure: Spread a clean, well-ironed cloth with the centre fold running down the middle of the table.
Allow about 60 cm width for each cover.
Place cutlery in order of use from the outside inwards: knives and soup spoon on the right (blades facing in), forks on the left, dessert spoon and fork above the plate position.
Place the bottom of the cutlery about 1-2 cm from the table edge; put the side plate on the left with the side knife, and the glass above the tip of the dinner knife.
Fold napkins neatly and place in the centre of the cover or on the side plate; add cruet and a low centrepiece.
Set a tray: clean tray cloth, all items needed for the meal within easy reach, a small flower, nothing overcrowded.
practicals.expectedObservations: A correctly set table looks balanced and uncluttered; cutlery lines are straight and every guest has the same arrangement. The invalid's tray is light, neat and attractive.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Each cover needs about 60 cm. For 8 guests seated 4 on each long side: 4 x 60 = 240 cm per side, so a table at least 2.4 m long is needed (plus space at the ends if hosts sit there).
precautions: Handle cutlery by the handles and glasses by the stems or base.
Keep the centrepiece low so guests can see each other.
sourcesOfError: Small tables reduce cover width.
commonMistakes: Putting forks on the right or knife blades facing outwards.
Laying cutlery for courses that are not being served.
Overcrowding the tray.
examTips: Draw and label a cover clearly when asked; examiners check positions of each item.
Know basic etiquette: serve from the left, clear from the right, wait for everyone before eating.

checkQuestions.q: Where is the soup spoon placed in a cover?
options: On the left outside the forks
On the right outside the knives
checkQuestions.explanation: Soup is the first course, so its spoon goes on the outside right.

checkQuestions.q: How much table width is usually allowed for one cover?
checkQuestions.explanation: About 60 cm per cover.

checkQuestions.q: Cutlery is laid
options: from the inside outwards in order of use
from the outside inwards in order of use
checkQuestions.explanation: Guests start with the outermost cutlery.

practicals.title: Making rechauffe dishes from leftover rice and fish
practicals.aim: To prepare attractive, safe dishes from leftover cooked rice and fish (fried rice and fish cakes).
materials: Leftover cooked rice (stored in a refrigerator)
safety: Use leftovers that were cooled quickly and refrigerated within 2 hours of cooking.
Reheat only once, until piping hot throughout (at least 75 °C).
procedure: Check that the leftovers smell and look normal and have been stored covered in the refrigerator for not more than 1-2 days.
Fried rice: stir-fry diced vegetables in a little oil, add the cold rice and seasoning, toss until piping hot.
Fish cakes: flake the fish, remove bones, mix with mashed potato, seasoning and a little egg to bind.
Shape into cakes, coat with egg and breadcrumbs, and shallow-fry until golden on both sides.
Check the centre is hot, garnish and serve at once.
practicals.expectedObservations: The dishes look and taste different from the original meal; added vegetables and coatings improve colour, flavour and texture.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Saving: 600 g of leftover cooked rice equals about 600 / 2.5 = 240 g of raw rice (rice roughly 2.5 times its weight on cooking). At N2,000 per kg, this is 0.24 x 2,000 = N480 of rice that is not wasted.
precautions: Never reheat food more than once.
Add fresh ingredients to improve nutritive value and flavour.
Season well, as reheated food can be bland.
sourcesOfError: The cooked-to-raw ratio for rice varies with the variety and amount of water.
commonMistakes: Keeping leftovers at room temperature for many hours.
Reheating until just warm.
Serving the leftover in the same form as before.
examTips: State rules for using leftovers: store properly, reheat thoroughly once, add fresh foods, season well, serve attractively.
Name a rechauffe dish for each leftover given in the question.

checkQuestions.q: Leftover food should be reheated
checkQuestions.explanation: Reheat once to at least 75 °C throughout.

checkQuestions.q: Which is a rechauffe dish made from leftover fish?
checkQuestions.explanation: Fish cakes use cooked, flaked leftover fish.

checkQuestions.q: 600 g of cooked rice comes from about how much raw rice (ratio 2.5)?

practicals.title: Festive dishes: small chops for a naming ceremony
practicals.aim: To plan, scale and prepare small chops (puff-puff, samosa or spring rolls, and peppered chicken) for a special occasion.
safety: Keep a lid or fire blanket near hot oil.
Do not leave frying unattended.
procedure: Decide the number of guests and pieces per guest; scale each recipe.
Make puff-puff batter (flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg, warm water); leave to rise until doubled.
Prepare the samosa filling and wrap the samosas neatly.
Season, boil and fry the chicken, then toss in pepper sauce.
Fry puff-puff by dropping small balls of batter into moderately hot oil; drain.
Arrange attractively on trays with toothpicks and serve.
practicals.expectedObservations: Puff-puff is round, golden and light inside; samosas are crisp and sealed; chicken is evenly coated. Presentation is colourful and suited to the occasion.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 30 guests at 3 puff-puff each: 30 x 3 = 90 pieces. If 250 g flour makes 30 puff-puff, flour needed = 90 / 30 x 250 = 750 g.
precautions: Keep oil at a moderate, steady temperature so the inside cooks.
Prepare items that can be made ahead to save time on the day.
sourcesOfError: Ball size varies, changing the number of puff-puff.
commonMistakes: Making far too much or too little because the recipe was not scaled.
Frying in oil that is too hot, giving raw centres.
examTips: Link the dishes to the occasion and give reasons.
Show scaling calculations clearly.

checkQuestions.q: If 250 g of flour makes 30 puff-puff, how much flour makes 90?
Which raising agent is used in puff-puff?
checkQuestions.explanation: Puff-puff is a yeast batter.

checkQuestions.q: Small chops are best described as
checkQuestions.explanation: They are bite-sized finger foods.

practicals.title: Improving a dish made from convenience foods
practicals.aim: To prepare a nutritious, attractive dish from instant noodles and compare its cost and preparation time with a home-made alternative.
safety: Read labels for expiry date and allergen information.
Check cans for dents, rust or bulging - discard if found.
procedure: Read and record the label information: ingredients, net mass, expiry date and cooking instructions.
Shred the vegetables and lightly stir-fry them.
Cook the noodles using only part of the seasoning sachet to reduce salt.
Add the vegetables and scrambled egg or sardines; toss together.
Time the preparation and serve attractively.
Compare cost and time with a dish made from basic ingredients.
practicals.expectedObservations: The improved noodle dish is ready in about 15 minutes and has better colour, protein and vitamins than plain noodles.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Noodles: 3 packs x 70 g = 210 g. Illustrative cost: noodles 3 x N300 = N900; eggs 2 x N200 = N400; vegetables N500; oil N100. Total = N1,900, or 1,900 / 3 = N633.33 per serving. Time: 15 minutes, compared with about 60 minutes for a home-made pasta and sauce.
precautions: Use part of the seasoning only - it is high in salt.
Check expiry dates before purchase.
sourcesOfError: Prices vary by brand and market.
commonMistakes: Serving convenience foods without adding vegetables or protein.
Ignoring "best before" and "use by" dates.
examTips: Give advantages (saves time, energy, easy storage) and disadvantages (cost, additives, salt, less variety).
Classify convenience foods: canned, dried, frozen, instant, ready-to-eat.

checkQuestions.q: One advantage of convenience foods is that they
checkQuestions.explanation: They save preparation time and fuel.

checkQuestions.q: A can of food should be rejected if it is
checkQuestions.explanation: Bulging may indicate gas from bacterial growth.

checkQuestions.q: How can the nutritive value of instant noodles be improved?
checkQuestions.explanation: Vegetables and egg add vitamins, minerals and protein.

practicals.title: Experiment: replacing wheat flour with cassava flour in chin-chin
practicals.aim: To investigate the effect of replacing 0%, 25% and 50% of wheat flour with high-quality cassava flour on the quality of chin-chin.
safety: Fry in small batches and keep a lid near the pot.
procedure: Prepare three batches, each with 400 g total flour and identical other ingredients.
Batch A: 400 g wheat flour; Batch B: 300 g wheat + 100 g cassava (25%); Batch C: 200 g wheat + 200 g cassava (50%).
Rub in the fat, add sugar, nutmeg, egg and milk to form a firm dough.
Roll to the same thickness, cut into equal cubes and fry until golden.
Code the samples and ask a panel of 5 tasters to score colour, crunchiness, taste and overall acceptability on a 5-point scale.
Calculate the mean score for each batch and conclude.
practicals.expectedObservations: Chin-chin with 25% cassava flour is similar to the wheat control; at 50% it may be slightly harder and paler. Composite flour reduces the amount of imported wheat used.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Flour amounts: 25% of 400 g = 100 g cassava + 300 g wheat; 50% = 200 g each. Overall acceptability scores (5 tasters): A [4, 4, 5, 4, 3] mean = 20/5 = 4.0; B [4, 5, 4, 3, 4] mean = 20/5 = 4.0; C [3, 3, 4, 2, 3] mean = 15/5 = 3.0. Conclusion: up to 25% replacement is as acceptable as pure wheat chin-chin.
precautions: Change only one variable (the flour mix).
Use coded samples so tasters are not biased.
Give tasters water between samples.
sourcesOfError: Small taste panel.
Differences in frying time and oil temperature.
commonMistakes: Changing more than one ingredient at once.
Not recording results in a table.
examTips: Write up experiments under aim, materials, method, results, conclusion.
Mention the importance of research in developing local recipes.

checkQuestions.q: In 400 g of composite flour with 25% cassava, how much cassava flour is used?
Why are the samples coded with letters or numbers?
options: To prevent tasters from being biased
checkQuestions.explanation: Coding hides the identity of each sample.

practicals.title: Improving a local recipe: soya-enriched pap (ogi)
practicals.topic: Research into Local Dishes and Drinks
practicals.aim: To improve the nutritive value of pap (ogi/akamu) by adding soya bean flour and to calculate the change in protein.
safety: Pour boiling water carefully while stirring.
Use soya flour that has been properly roasted or cooked - raw soya contains substances that reduce protein digestion.
procedure: Collect information on how ogi is traditionally prepared and its nutritive value.
Prepare plain pap from 100 g ogi as the control.
Prepare enriched pap by mixing 80 g ogi with 20 g roasted soya flour, blending with cold water, then adding boiling water while stirring until it thickens.
Taste both and compare colour, flavour, consistency and acceptability.
Use food composition values to calculate the protein in each.
Write a short report recommending the improved recipe.
practicals.expectedObservations: The soya-enriched pap is slightly creamier in colour with a nutty flavour; most tasters find it acceptable. It contains much more protein than plain pap.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Protein per 100 g (given): maize ogi 9.4 g; soya flour 36 g. Plain pap (100 g ogi): 9.4 g protein. Enriched pap: 80 g ogi = 80 x 9.4/100 = 7.52 g; 20 g soya = 20 x 36/100 = 7.2 g; total = 14.72 g. Increase = (14.72 - 9.4)/9.4 x 100 = 56.6%.
precautions: Blend with cold water first to avoid lumps.
Use clean water and utensils as pap is often fed to infants.
sourcesOfError: Composition values vary with maize variety and fermentation.
commonMistakes: Adding raw soya flour.
Forgetting a control for comparison.
examTips: Show how the recipe was improved: nutritive value, method, time/energy, presentation.
State the importance of research in foods and nutrition.
